meta.title: MedFact: Benchmarking the Fact-Checking Capabilities of LLMs on Chinese Medical Texts
meta.subtitle: A diverse, uncontaminated benchmark for safe medical AI
meta.authors: Jiayi He, Yangmin Huang, Qianyun Du, Xiangying Zhou, Zhiyang He, Jiaxue Hu, Xiaodong Tao, Lixian Lai

slides.notes: Welcome. Today I'll present MedFact, a benchmark for testing whether large language models can fact-check Chinese medical text. The core question: can LLMs reliably catch medical errors well enough to be safe in healthcare? Spoiler: not yet, and they fail in an interesting way we call over-criticism.

slides.title: Medical LLMs need rigorous fact-checking
bullets: LLMs increasingly draft and answer **medical content**
A single factual error can **harm patients**
Deployment demands **regulatory compliance**, not just fluency
Existing benchmarks test QA, not **error detection in real text**
We need to know: can models **catch medical errors**?
slides.notes: The motivation is patient safety. As LLMs write and answer medical questions, factual errors carry real clinical risk. Most prior work measures question-answering accuracy, but fact-checking existing text is a distinct, deployment-critical skill that was under-evaluated. MedFact targets exactly this gap.

slides.title: What this paper delivers
bullets: Evaluation of **20 leading LLMs** on two tasks
Models trail **human experts**, especially on localization
slides.notes: Three contributions. First, the MedFact benchmark itself, built to be diverse and resistant to data contamination. Second, a broad evaluation of 20 LLMs showing they fall short of humans, particularly on pinpointing errors. Third, the over-criticism phenomenon, where models flag correct text as wrong, made worse by advanced reasoning techniques.

slides.title: A hybrid AI-human construction pipeline
bullets: **7-LLM filter** by majority vote, Fleiss κ 0.75
Filtered to **6,405**, then hard-case mining + augmentation
slides.figure_caption: Figure 1: Data construction pipeline and MedFact components.
slides.notes: Construction is the technical heart of the paper. We begin with a private corpus so models haven't seen it. A seven-LLM ensemble filters for difficulty and quality, refined over three expert-in-the-loop rounds that lifted filter-expert agreement to 96.4%. Hard-case mining, similarity filtering, and de-identifying augmentation yield a balanced final set of 2,116 instances: half correct, half with a single injected error.

slides.title: Broad, realistic coverage
bullets: Led by **Internal Medicine** (~55%), then OB-GYN, Surgery
**4 writing styles**: encyclopedia, journalism, Q&A, misinformation
**5 difficulty levels** by model success rate
slides.figure_caption: Figure 3: Distribution of specialties in MedFact.
slides.notes: MedFact is deliberately diverse. It spans 13 specialties grouped into four domains, with a realistic skew toward internal medicine that matches the source corpus. It also varies writing style from formal encyclopedia entries to fabricated misinformation, and is stratified into five difficulty bands. This breadth is what lets us measure generalizable fact-checking, not style-specific tricks.

slides.title: Errors are overwhelmingly medical
slides.figure_caption: Table 1: Distribution of 8 fine-grained error types (1,058 incorrect instances).
slides.notes: We designed an eight-type taxonomy with medical experts, split into medical and non-medical errors. Almost 90% are medical, with conceptual errors alone over half. The key implication: succeeding on MedFact requires genuine medical understanding, not surface-level cues. This is why the benchmark is hard.

slides.title: Two tasks: detect, then localize

columns.text: Binary: is the text correct or incorrect?

slides.notes: Two tasks of increasing difficulty. Veracity Classification just asks if the text has an error. Error Localization asks the model to point to the exact wrong span, only scored when the text was correctly flagged. EL is the strict probe of medical knowledge. We use GPT-4o as an automated EL judge, validated at Cohen's kappa around 0.87 against three medical professionals.

slides.title: Models detect errors, but can't localize them
bullets: Every model scores **lower on EL than VC**
slides.notes: Headline numbers. Proprietary models lead; Doubao-Seed-1.6-thinking is the top general model and XiaoYi the top medical one. But the best EL F1 of 0.686 still trails the human 0.701, and every model drops from VC to EL. Models often classify text as wrong for the wrong reason, fingering a sound statement as the error. Localization is the honest test of medical knowledge.

slides.title: Full results: 20 LLMs, zero-shot and CoT
slides.figure_caption: Table 3: Full MedFact results (zero-shot & CoT). Best bold, 2nd-best underlined; human = avg of 3 professionals.
slides.notes: Here is the full table. Look down the EL columns: even the best proprietary models with chain-of-thought sit below the human row at the top. The VC-to-EL gap is visible across the board. Open-source medical models like II-Medical-8B and HuatuoGPT struggle most on localization, underscoring that scale and specialization alone don't close the knowledge gap.

slides.title: Failures are knowledge failures
bullets: **~76% of DeepSeek-R1 errors**: insufficient medical knowledge
**Concept conflation** of related drugs or conditions
slides.figure_caption: Figure 4: Error distribution of DeepSeek-R1 and XiaoYi on the EL task (zero-shot).
slides.notes: Expert error analysis shows the dominant failure, about 76% for DeepSeek-R1, is simply insufficient medical knowledge. Within that we see concept conflation, reliance on outdated guidelines that read plausibly, and logical inconsistencies where the reasoning and verdict disagree. The takeaway: improve underlying medical knowledge, fine-grained discrimination, and reasoning consistency, rather than just adding compute.

slides.title: Advanced reasoning makes models over-critical
bullets: **RAG helps** both tasks with relevant sources
Same **'precision down, recall up'** across all 5 models
Agents reward **flagging novel errors**, not concurrence
slides.figure_caption: Figure 8: Precision/recall changes after applying MAD and MDAgents.
slides.notes: This is the paper's most striking finding. Retrieval helps when sources are relevant. But multi-agent debate, MAD and MDAgents, systematically pushes recall up and precision down across all five models tested. Each agent is rewarded for proposing a novel error, so aggregation amplifies false positives. We call this over-criticism. Inference-time budget-forcing shows the same pattern: more deliberation, more hallucinated errors, no real gain.

slides.title: Over-criticism persists across languages
bullets: Models flag errors **more aggressively in English**
slides.notes: We checked whether over-criticism is a quirk of Chinese. On an English-translated MedFact, both Doubao and Gemini improve in F1 and recall, but Doubao's precision falls, meaning more false positives. So over-criticism is cross-lingual, not language-specific. Language materially shifts the precision-recall balance, which matters for any multilingual medical deployment.

slides.title: What to remember
bullets: Models **detect** errors but **can't localize** them like humans
Failures are **medical-knowledge** failures, not reasoning style
For safety, **prioritize knowledge** and balanced precision-recall
slides.notes: To summarize: MedFact is a diverse, contamination-resistant Chinese medical fact-checking benchmark. Across 20 LLMs, models can detect errors but fall short of humans on localization. The bottleneck is medical knowledge, and advanced reasoning techniques can backfire via over-criticism. For safe medical AI, invest in knowledge and watch the precision-recall trade-off rather than just adding deliberation.

slides.title: Scope and responsible release
bullets: EL uses a **GPT-4o judge** (scalable, but imperfect)
Medical knowledge is **fixed at creation time**
IRB-approved; **all PII removed**; fair annotator pay
**Research-only** license: no clinical or commercial use
slides.notes: Honest limitations: the benchmark is Chinese-specific, the EL judge is an LLM with its own biases, and medical knowledge can age. Ethically, we obtained IRB approval, removed all PII, and paid annotators fairly. Because incorrect instances could be misused, we release under a restrictive research-only license that prohibits clinical and commercial deployment. Thank you, happy to take questions.
